issues.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition of a capital asset constitutes a transfer for the purpose of imposing capital gains tax.
material_facts: An electricity undertaking was acquired by the government under statutory authority, and its properties vested in the government.
The former owner received compensation, and the tax authority treated the amount exceeding the value of the fixed assets as capital gains.
The acquisition extinguished the former owner’s title and vested the property in the government.
issues.conclusion: The compulsory acquisition was a transfer within the meaning of section 12B(1), so any taxable surplus arising from it fell within the capital gains provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12B(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 uses “transfer” broadly to include voluntary and involuntary transfers. Its earlier proviso expressly excluded transfers resulting from compulsory acquisition, showing that such acquisitions were otherwise within the term; deletion of that exclusion confirmed the legislative intent. Extinguishment of an existing title and creation of a new title constitutes a transfer. The Court approved Commissioner of Income-tax v. Shrikrishan Chandmal, Wilfred Pereira Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Commissioner of Income-tax v. United India Life Assurance Company Ltd., and Vadilal Soda Ice Factory v. Commissioner of Income-tax.

predicates.capital_gains_assessment_case: The proceeding concerns whether a gain is taxable as a capital gain.
predicates.compulsory_acquisition_of_capital_asset: The government acquired a person’s capital asset under compulsory legal authority.
predicates.existing_title_extinguished_and_new_titl: The acquisition extinguished the former owner’s title and created title in another.

issues.definition: When a capital-gains assessment concerns a compulsory acquisition that extinguishes an existing title and creates a new one, the acquisition counts as a transfer for capital-gains purposes.

issues.legal_issue: The general term “transfer” is not restricted to voluntary transfers by applying the ejusdem generis rule to its association with “sale,” “exchange,” and “relinquishment.”
material_facts: The associated terms ordinarily refer to voluntary acts, but the Court found no distinct genus or category that could limit the broader term “transfer.”
issues.conclusion: The ejusdem generis rule did not apply to restrict “transfer” to voluntary acts; the listed terms were to be given their plain and natural meanings.
issues.legal_principle: The ejusdem generis rule is a presumption of construction, not an automatic rule, and requires a distinct genus or category. The Court relied on Craies on Statute Law and quoted with approval Provost, etc. of Glasgow v. Glasgow Tramway Co. and N.A.L.G.O. v. Bolton Corporation.

predicates.statutory_interpretation_case: The proceeding requires the court to interpret a general term used alongside more specific terms.
predicates.broad_general_term: The disputed term has a meaning broad enough to cover different kinds of acts.
predicates.no_distinct_genus_in_associated_terms: The associated terms do not identify a distinct class or category that encompasses the disputed term.

issues.definition: When a broad general term appears with associated terms that do not identify a distinct class, the general term is not restricted by the ejusdem generis rule.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to exclude compensation attributable to goodwill cannot be entertained when it was not raised before the initial tax authorities and no material was provided to value the goodwill or apportion compensation to it.
material_facts: The taxpayer did not claim before the assessing officer or the first appellate authority that goodwill was not a capital asset or that compensation attributable to goodwill should be excluded.
The taxpayer raised a goodwill-apportionment contention before the tribunal but provided no material from which goodwill could be valued or compensation apportioned.
The question whether any compensation was attributable to goodwill was a mixed question of law and fact.
issues.conclusion: The taxpayer could not raise the goodwill-apportionment contention in the further proceedings, and the rejection of that contention was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A mixed question of law and fact concerning the value of goodwill and the portion of compensation attributable to it requires supporting material. Where the issue was not raised before the initial tax authorities and the taxpayer provided no valuation or apportionment material before the tribunal, the contention could not be entertained in the reference proceedings under section 256(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

predicates.goodwill_tax_reference_appeal: The proceeding is a tax reference appeal concerning whether compensation attributable to goodwill should be excluded from capital gains.
predicates.goodwill_claim_not_raised_before_initial: The taxpayer did not raise the goodwill exclusion claim before the assessing officer or the first appellate authority.
predicates.goodwill_claim_raised_before_tribunal: The taxpayer raised the goodwill exclusion claim before the tribunal.
predicates.no_material_to_value_or_apportion_goodwi: The taxpayer provided no material from which goodwill could be valued or compensation apportioned to it.

issues.definition: In a goodwill tax reference appeal, a claim first raised before the tribunal cannot be entertained if no valuation or apportionment material is provided.
